AP-YonhapJapan's financial regulator has moved to block domestic sales of leveraged exchange-traded funds tied to individual Japanese stocks such as Kioxia and Toyota Motor, products that U.S. asset managers are lining up to launch. The regulator concluded that allowing high-risk products barred at home to enter through overseas markets could amplify price swings in specific stocks and distort normal price formation in the market.Japan's Financial Services Agency revised its Q&A on financial instruments business the previous day, setting out its official position on domestic sales of Japan single-stock leveraged ETFs established abroad, according to Nihon Keizai Shimbun and other outlets on the 29th.The agency said it was "not appropriate from a public interest standpoint" for Japanese financial firms to sell such overseas-created products. It cited concerns that they could amplify price movements in individual stocks listed on the Japanese market and significantly affect price formation in the country's financial markets.Trading of leveraged ETFs based on individual Japanese stocks is not currently permitted on Japanese exchanges. Unlike index-based leveraged ETFs, products that track twice the daily move of a single company's shares cannot be traded on the domestic market.The measure comes as U.S. asset managers prepare a series of leveraged ETF launches targeting major Japanese companies.Turtle Capital Management, ProShares and Tidal Financial Group, among other U.S. managers, have recently filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission to list leveraged ETFs based on Kioxia shares. Products tracking Toyota Motor, Sony Group and SoftBank Group are also preparing to enter the U.S. market.Leveraged ETFs are designed to deliver two times or more the daily return of a particular stock or index. Gains are magnified when the underlying asset rises, but losses can mount just as quickly when it falls.The effect on the broader market is another concern. Managers must adjust their holdings of derivatives or underlying assets every trading day to maintain the target multiple. If buying or selling becomes concentrated on one side during that process, it can widen swings in the underlying shares themselves.What Japan is most wary of is indirect sales routed through overseas markets. Even products that cannot be listed directly in Japan could reach Japanese investors if they are first established in the United States or elsewhere and then handled by Japanese financial firms.With the Q&A revision, the agency has effectively put a stop to domestic handling of such foreign single-stock leveraged ETFs.The side effects of single-stock leveraged products that surfaced first in South Korea are also cited as heightening market caution. In May, single-stock leveraged ETFs and exchange-traded notes based on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix were listed for the first time. As retail trading grew rapidly, concerns mounted that the products could amplify price swings in the underlying shares.South Korean regulators responded by suspending new listings of single-stock leveraged products and tightening rules, including raising the minimum deposit required of retail investors.The Financial Services Agency is seen as focusing on curbing the potential for greater market volatility by controlling sales at the earliest stage, before single-stock leveraged products flow into the Japanese market in earnest.#JapanFSA#LeveragedETF#Kioxia#ToyotaMotor#ETFRegulation#MarketVolatilityCompanies in this storySamsung Electronics005930.KS · SemiconductorAI KEY Company Analysis →Original reporting by Cho Su-yeon for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
